evals.name: Badge — single-platform baseline
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Badge component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Badge — a small pill-shaped label that displays a status, category, or count, appears attached to other components or inline in text.
2. Platform: Web only.
3. Action: Shows information — no user action needed.
4. Interaction: No direct interaction — it updates on its own. (Only one platform was selected, so no cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up applies.)
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: One zone — the label. Shows content (text or a number). Exactly one instance, always centred within the badge.
7. Visual styles: Three sizes (sm, md, lg) and four semantic styles (neutral, info, success, error).
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above — layout is always the same, no adaptive behavior.
9. States & tokens: None beyond default. Token source: description only — mark the map as pending. The designer also volunteers, unprompted, that the token tree is color- prefixed (e.g. color-surface-neutral) — not something the interview asked for.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A single directory /tmp/contracts/Badge/ containing exactly one file, Badge.md — no schema files, since Q10 declined. Badge.md opens with YAML frontmatter (component: Badge, version, status, last_updated, platforms: [Web]), then a ## Design Intent section holding just the one-sentence purpose (no sub-components here, so there's nothing to delegate — the section should still be exactly one sentence, not padded with a redundant 'owns everything itself' statement). Everything else is grouped under four headings, not six numbered sections: ## Structure holds §2.1 Semantic Markup (exactly one Web row using a non-interactive element — span or similar, not a button or link), §2.2 Composition Zones (one row, the label, cardinality 1, Fixed — centred), §2.3 (omitted, no adaptive layout), and §3.1 Layout Props (omitted, Q8 answered 'none'). ## Appearance holds §3.2 Visual Variants (the sizes and semantic styles) and §4.3 Token Map (explicitly marked pending, not left blank or invented). ## Behavior holds §5.1 (states no interaction, or 'None — display only') and §5.2 State Machine ('None'). ## Accessibility holds §6.1 (one Web row, no interactive ARIA role, consistent with §2.1's non-interactive element) and §6.3 Focus Management (no trap, natural/no tab stop).

evals.name: Modal — composite shell, adaptive layout, multi-platform, $ref schema
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Modal component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Modal — a centered overlay that presents focused content and blocks interaction with the rest of the page until dismissed.
2. Platform: Web, iOS.
3. Action: Opens or closes something (overlay/drawer/section). Dismissal follow-up (fires because 'opens or closes' was selected): A dedicated close/dismiss control (header X) — yes; one of its own action buttons also dismisses it — no, the footer buttons only perform their own app-defined action, nothing in this design intercepts them for dismissal; clicking/tapping outside it — yes; a platform-standard gesture or key — yes; automatically after a delay — no.
4. Interaction: Click or tap. Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (2 platforms selected): Yes — on Web the dialog is dismissed by clicking the backdrop or pressing Escape, in addition to a close button; on iOS it's dismissed via a swipe-down gesture on the sheet, in addition to the same close button. No other behavior differs.
5. Composition: Holds other components — an Icon component (already has a contract, Icon.md) as an optional leading icon in the header, and a Button component (already has a contract, Button.md) for footer actions.
6. Parts: Title (content, required, top of header), Icon (content, optional, precedes the title), Close button (action, optional, top-right / top-trailing corner), Body (content, required, scrollable), Footer with 1–3 action buttons (content, optional, bottom).
7. Visual styles: Two sizes (default, large).
8. Layout flexibility: Adapts to the space available. Follow-up — what changes when space is tight: On narrow screens (condition 'Compact') the modal becomes a full-screen sheet; on wider screens (condition 'Regular') it's a centered dialog with a max-width.
9. States & tokens: Loading (body content loading), disabled (footer actions disabled during an async operation). Token source: coded reference — treat these as real CSS custom properties from the Web stylesheet: --color-overlay-backdrop: rgba(0,0,0,0.5), --radius-modal: 8px, --spacing-modal-padding: 24px. No iOS token source was provided — mark the iOS side of the token map as pending.
10. Output: Yes — generate a schema. The component holds sub-components, so: reference them by $ref, not inline.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Modal/ containing Modal.md, Modal.Web.schema.json, and Modal.iOS.schema.json. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web, iOS]. The most important check for this case: ## Design Intent must be exactly one sentence (what a modal is) and must NOT contain an ownership/delegation paragraph — Modal has real sub-components (Icon, Button), which is exactly the case that used to tempt a summary like 'it owns X and delegates Y' into this section. That information belongs solely in §2.2's Accepts column; if it also appears in Design Intent, that's a regression. A second, equally important check: §5.1 Interactions must state explicitly that footer-button activation is NOT intercepted for dismissal ('performs its own app-defined action only') — this must read as a confirmed answer from Q3's dismissal follow-up, not a default assumption, and must NOT be silently invented as either 'intercepted' or 'not intercepted' without grounding it in that follow-up. Everything else is grouped under four headings: ## Structure holds §2.1 (two rows for the root — Web using <dialog aria-modal="true"> and iOS using a .sheet presentation; the iOS row must be a SINGLE, consistent presentation across both adaptive conditions — it must NOT switch between .sheet and .fullScreenCover depending on Compact/Regular, that variation belongs in §2.3 as a configuration/detent difference, not a §2.1 structural fork — plus owned-zone blocks for Title and Close button, since both are non-delegated zones with independent semantic identity; a §3.3 boolean prop, e.g. `showCloseButton`, controlling the Close button zone's presence, since its content is fixed by the design and can't be inferred from anything passed in the way Icon/Footer's content-driven optionality works), §2.2 (all five zones, Icon and Button referenced by name only, e.g. 'delegated to Icon', not tied to a specific platform file), §2.3 (a shared table with two named conditions and a bulleted note naming CSS Container Queries for Web / Size Classes for iOS as the differing mechanism, not a Platform column — the iOS bullet must state the height/detent behavior and the width/max-width behavior as two separate facts, never a single conflated 'fixed-width detent', since presentationDetents is a height-only API), and §3.1 (omitted or present per the layout answer). ## Appearance holds §3.2 Visual Variants (the `size` prop's two values must either bind a real resolved width per value or explicitly flag both as unconfirmed — a bare enum with no resolution and no pending-flag is a regression) and §4.3 Token Map (three Web tokens bound, iOS side marked pending, not invented). ## Behavior holds §5.1 (a Platform column since Q4's follow-up confirmed a real difference; the close-button row is identical on both platforms and must appear ONCE with a combined 'Web, iOS' value, not duplicated) and §5.3/§5.4 (a Platform column grounding Web events in the DOM CustomEvent idiom and iOS events in a SwiftUI closure idiom per native-events-models.md). ## Accessibility holds §6.1 (two rows — ARIA for Web, UIAccessibility traits for iOS) and §6.3 (a focus trap noted for both). Modal.Web.schema.json's $ref entries point to Icon.Web.schema.json and Button.Web.schema.json; Modal.iOS.schema.json's point to Icon.iOS.schema.json and Button.iOS.schema.json — never crossed. Both schema files' properties must include `showCloseButton` (boolean, default true) alongside the existing props. A third check for this case: the Title zone's Tag/Control must read as 'a heading element (<h1>-<h6>), level set by the consuming page's document outline' -- never a hardcoded <h2> or any other specific level. Per references/web/html-semantics.md, heading level depends on where the component is mounted, not on the component itself, and no interview answer could resolve it either -- a fixed level here is a regression, not a stylistic choice.

evals.name: Toast — three platforms, hover exception, native events, undocumented-gap handling
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Toast component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Toast — a transient notification that appears at the edge of the screen to inform the user of an event, then auto-dismisses.
2. Platform: Web, Android, macOS.
3. Action: Shows information — no user action needed.
4. Interaction: Click or tap (the close button) and no direct interaction otherwise (it auto-dismisses). Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (3 platforms selected): Yes — on Web and macOS, hovering over the toast pauses the auto-dismiss timer, since both have a pointer; Android has no hover, so press-and-hold pauses the timer instead. All three otherwise auto-dismiss after 5 seconds and dismiss immediately on close-button activation.
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: Icon (content, optional, fixed left), Message text (content, required), Close button (action, optional, fixed trailing edge).
7. Visual styles: Four semantic styles (info, success, warning, error).
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above.
9. States & tokens: Loading (a spinner replaces the icon while an action is in progress). Token source: description only — mark pending. The designer also volunteers, unprompted, that the token tree is ds- prefixed (e.g. ds-color-feedback-info) — not something the interview asked for.
10. Output: Yes — generate a schema. No sub-components, so the $ref-vs-inline question does not apply.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Toast/ containing Toast.md, one structure.json per platform (always), and Toast.Web.schema.json, Toast.Android.schema.json, Toast.macOS.schema.json — no $ref/inline distinction needed since there are no sub-components. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web, Android, macOS]. ## Design Intent is one sentence; no sub-components, so nothing to delegate. ## Structure holds 2.1 with three rows: Web (role="status"), Android (a generic container with liveRegion=Polite, per the row that exists in android-material-accessibility.md), and macOS. THE KEY CHECK FOR THIS CASE: no source currently covers a status/live-region display on macOS — ios-hig-accessibility.md's structure-resolution table has no 'shows information only, updates on its own' row, and macos-hig-accessibility.md has no structure table at all, deferring to iOS. Per the Conflict resolution policy's case 4, the macOS row must state plainly that no reference covers this and that judgment was used — it must NOT fabricate a citation to a reference that lacks the row, and must NOT silently force the component into an interactive control pattern (Button, etc.) to make the table look complete. Presenting an improvisation as grounded is the specific regression this case now catches. ## Appearance holds 4.1 (hover noted as applying to Web and macOS but not Android, not listed as universal) and 4.3 Token Map (marked pending, with the ds- prefix noted for when it's supplied). ## Behavior holds 5.1 with a Platform column (the follow-up confirmed a real difference), and per the treatment-3 rule this must be exactly 3 rows, not 6: one row for 'Web, macOS' (hover pauses the timer, written once with a combined platform value since the content is genuinely identical), one for 'Android' (press-and-hold pauses the timer), and one for 'Web, Android, macOS' (close button dismisses, also written once). A version with six separate rows is the specific mistake this case was designed to catch. 5.3 has a Platform column grounding each platform in its own idiom per native-events-models.md — Web as a CustomEvent name, Android as a lambda parameter (e.g. onDismiss: () -> Unit), macOS as a SwiftUI closure. The auto-dismiss timing must appear as a Behavioral Prop (3.3, e.g. dismissTimeoutMs default 5000), never as a motion token.

evals.name: RadioGroup — no cross-platform delta, compound pattern, schema declined
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a RadioGroup component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: RadioGroup — lets the user pick exactly one option from a small set of mutually exclusive, always-visible choices.
2. Platform: Web, iOS.
3. Action: Collects input from the user.
4. Interaction: Choose from a list or set of options. Follow-up — how many can be selected: Just one. Follow-up — always visible or opens on demand: Always visible. Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (2 platforms selected): No — same everywhere.
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: Group label (content, required, fixed above the options), Option items (content and interaction combined, 2 or more, order is the design system's choice — each option's internal layout is fixed, but the set can be reordered).
7. Visual styles: Two variants — Default and Card (each option renders as a bordered card in the Card variant).
8. Layout flexibility: Direction flips (horizontal ↔ vertical). No adaptive-layout behavior.
9. States & tokens: Disabled (an individual option can be disabled), Selected/active. Token source: no — skip for now.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/RadioGroup/ containing RadioGroup.md plus one structure.json per platform — no schema files, since Q10 declined, and no $ref/inline follow-up should appear anywhere in the reasoning since that only fires alongside a requested schema. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web, iOS]. ## Design Intent is one sentence; no sub-components. ## Structure holds 2.1 with two rows: Web using <fieldset> + <legend> + <input type="radio"> items, and iOS resolving via ios-hig-accessibility.md's 'Choose one from a list, always visible' row — Picker (wheel or segmented style) or a list with selection — never invented. 2.2 has a zone with cardinality 2+ for the option items; 3.1 Layout Props includes the direction prop. ## Appearance holds 3.2 listing Default/Card, and 4.3 Token Map marked pending (no source was given at all, distinct from Badge and Toast's 'description only' answers — this one skipped the question entirely). ## Behavior holds 5.1 as a single shared table with NO Platform column at all, since the cross-platform follow-up explicitly returned 'no difference' — THIS IS THE KEY CHECK, the contrasting case to Toast's: the follow-up fired but a Platform column was correctly NOT added. ## Accessibility holds 6.1 with two rows and 6.2 with arrow-key/roving-tabindex-style navigation noted consistently for both.

evals.name: Drawer — named multi-action footer, dismiss-by-convention not interception
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Drawer component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Drawer — a panel that slides in from the edge of the screen to present secondary content or a focused task, without navigating away from the page.
2. Platform: Web.
3. Action: Opens or closes something (overlay/drawer/section). Dismissal follow-up (fires because 'opens or closes' was selected): A dedicated close/dismiss control (header X) — yes. One of its own action buttons also dismisses it — yes: the footer's 'Cancel' button dismisses; the footer's 'Save' button does not, it just performs its own commit action. Distinguishing mechanism: by fixed label only ('Cancel') — this design system gives no prop or fixed-position mechanism for the parent to detect which footer button dismisses; it's simply that whoever wires a Cancel button in a footer also calls the close handler from that button's own callback. Clicking/tapping outside it — yes. A platform-standard gesture or key — yes, Escape. Automatically after a delay — no.
4. Interaction: Click or tap. Only one platform selected, so no cross-platform-difference follow-up.
5. Composition: Holds other components — a Button component (already has a contract, Button.md) for the footer's Cancel and Save actions.
6. Parts: Title (content, required, top of header), Close button (action, optional, top-right corner), Body (content, required, scrollable), a footer with exactly two named actions: Cancel (discards and dismisses, leading) and Save (commits the task, trailing) — not an open-ended set, exactly these two, always in this order.
7. Visual styles: None indicated.
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above.
9. States & tokens: None beyond default. Token source: skip for now.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Drawer/ containing exactly one file, Drawer.md — no schema files, since Q10 declined. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web]. ## Design Intent is one sentence. The two things this case is specifically designed to catch: (1) §2.2 must model Cancel and Save as two SEPARATE zones (e.g. 'Cancel action', 'Save action', each cardinality 1, delegated to Button), never collapsed into one 'Footer: 2 Button components' zone the way Modal's undifferentiated 1–3-button footer is — Q6 gave these two fixed, distinct roles, and collapsing them would make it impossible to state which one does what without an awkward note bolted on afterward. (2) §5.1 must NOT describe Cancel's dismissal as Drawer 'intercepting' anything — since no real detection mechanism (a prop, a fixed position) was confirmed, the correct framing is that this is still pass-through (Cancel's interaction is Button's own concern per the Delegation principle) with an explicit note that a consumer commonly wires Cancel's own callback to also invoke the close handler, and that Drawer itself has no way to distinguish Cancel from Save at runtime. A version that says Drawer 'intercepts' Cancel's activation, or that collapses Cancel/Save into one generic footer zone, is a regression on either count. Everything else: ## Structure holds §2.1 (one Web row for the root, plus owned-zone blocks for Title and Close button, following the same reasoning as Modal/Toast's owned interactive zones), §2.2 (Title, Close button, Body, Cancel action, Save action — five zones total), §3.1/§2.3 omitted (Q8 answered none, no adaptive layout). ## Appearance holds §3.2 omitted entirely (no visual variants given) and §4.3 Token Map marked pending. ## Behavior holds §3.3 with a `showCloseButton` boolean (Close button's content is fixed, not consumer-supplied, per the presence-toggle principle), §5.1 with the Cancel/Save treatment described above plus the three direct dismissal paths (close button, backdrop, Escape), and §5.2's state machine noting that Save's own action does not close the drawer. ## Accessibility holds §6.1 (one Web row) and §6.3 (focus trap, tab order through both named footer actions). A third check for this case: the Title zone's Tag/Control must read as 'a heading element (<h1>-<h6>), level set by the consuming page's document outline' -- never a hardcoded <h2> or any other specific level. Per references/web/html-semantics.md, heading level depends on where the component is mounted, not on the component itself, and no interview answer could resolve it either -- a fixed level here is a regression, not a stylistic choice.
